subject: ventures/container-load-planner
professional: a freight forwarder's load planner who books FCL and FTL space and signs off stuffing plans; first checks: does the count respect the payload, does the floor pattern for Euro and 48x40 pallets match what fits (mixed lengthwise/crosswise rows), are stacking and fragile limits honoured, does anything exceed the door aperture, is the weight spread so the centre of gravity sits near the middle (and within road limits once on a chassis), and are the equipment sizes the real inside dimensions

evidence.correctness: Recomputed by hand geometry and checked with `node /tmp/claude-0/audit-container/run.mjs` and `run2.mjs` (every plan also passed the shipped verifyPacking): 150 Euro pallets 120x80x85 cm, 250 kg: floor 25 in a 40 ft (10 lengthwise + 15 crosswise, 800+1200=2000 <= 2352 mm), floor(2393/850)=2 layers -> 50 and 3 containers; 40 HC floor(2698/850)=3 -> 75 and 2 (tool 50/3 and 75/2). 70 x 600 kg pallets: floor(26500/600)=44, second container 26 / 15,600 kg (tool 44/26, 26,400/15,600 kg). Floor-only Euro: 20 ft 4+7=11, 40 ft 25 (tool 11, 25). Floor-only 48x40 in: 40 ft 9+11=20, 20 ft 4+5=9 (tool 20 and 9). 53 ft trailer, 48x40 turned 40 in along the length: 15 rows x 2 = 30, the usual 'turned' trucking figure (tool 30); 26 ft truck 12 (tool 12). 60x40x40 cm upright cartons in a 20 ft: 14x3 + 9x1 = 51 per layer x 5 layers = 255 (tool 255). Presets: 20/40/40HC inside 5,898/12,032 x 2,352 x 2,393/2,698 mm are the commonly published manufacturer figures and exceed the ISO 1496-1 minimum inside sizes; payloads 28,200 / 26,500 kg are consistent with a 30,480 kg ISO 668 rating minus tare (standards from own knowledge, not fetched). I tried to beat the tool's 2-trailer answer for the built-in example in a 53 ft by hand (10 pallets 3-across at the doors, the rest packed in the front 11,354 mm): 810 of 870 units, so its answer is not refuted (glassware's 2-layer, 5 kg-on-top limit wastes the height above it). Not a 4: the 53 ft preset width 2,591 mm (102 in) is the legal outside width of a trailer, not the inside (about 99-101 in), and the 26 ft box truck is 7,300 mm long (about 24 ft); neither changed the pallet counts tested.
evidence.completeness: Claimed features run end to end: parse/units (metric and imperial), extreme-point packer with rotation, support, highest layer, weight on top and payload; multi-start search; greedy multi-container plan with tail merge and a volume/weight lower bound; palletise and the 'what if I swap' comparison over five presets loose and on pallets; quoted-rate pricing that never names an incomplete option cheapest; balance report; multi-drop stops (CLI); CSV loading list, printable HTML plan with disclaimer, share link (encodeShare/decodeShare); CLI (`node cli.mjs --example --rates 20ft=2400,40ft=3800,40hc=4000` printed plan, comparison and freight table; `--html` contains the No-warranty paragraph). Guide's worked example reproduces. No TODOs or stubs found. Served copy rewrites the github.io origin in llms.txt (`node platform/pages/served-copy.mjs container-load-planner`: no placeholder or retired origin left).
evidence.verification: `cd ventures/container-load-planner && node --test '*.test.mjs'`: 77 tests, 77 pass, 3.4 s; tests include hand-computed fits, an independent verifyPacking and random loads checked for overlap, bounds, weight, rotation, support and stacking. Seven non-equivalent mutants via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: payload check `weight + ln.weight >` -> `weight >` caught; minSupport 0.75 -> 0.5 caught; verifier skips support for z <= 300 caught; stopReport `<=` -> `<` caught; balance longTol 0.1 -> 0.2 SURVIVED; latTol doubled SURVIVED; 40 HC height 2698 -> 2598 SURVIVED (the guide's 3 x 850 mm still fits, so only the preset value is unpinned). A further stopReport mutant (`b.x < a.x + a.l` -> `b.x < a.x`) survived but is equivalent (an x-overlapping box with y/z overlap would already collide), so it is not counted. The packer core is well covered; the balance thresholds and preset dimensions are not.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (916 lines), cli.mjs, index.html script, calc.test.mjs. Pure integer-millimetre geometry, frozen presets, deterministic seeded RNG, a separate verifier, escaped HTML output, guarded storage, input caps (6,000 units, 40 lines). Defects: num() strips every comma (calc.mjs:68), so a decimal-comma weight '12,5' becomes 125 kg silently (`buildLine({weight:'12,5',...})` -> 125); the slide step pushes every unit to y = 0 (calc.mjs:344), so a narrow load (24 x 1,000 kg 1 m cubes in a 40 ft) is left-justified and the tool then warns that its own plan is 7% off-centre toward the left wall.
evidence.claims: Backed: guide worked example 50/3, 75/2, 44 + 26 at 26,400 / 15,600 kg (rerun above); FAQ '25 Euro pallets on the floor of a 40 ft', '11 Euro pallets in a 20 ft', 'about 20' 48x40 in a 40 ft (all reproduced); 'Not modelled' list (index.html:179) and no-warranty footer on both pages, README and the printable plan; privacy line vs usage.mjs (local-only, opt-out, Do Not Track honoured at usage.mjs:34); 'states no freight rate' (priceOptions only uses typed rates). Not backed: index.html:185 (and the FAQPage JSON-LD at :12) and how-to-plan-a-container-load.html:63 (JSON-LD :11) say a 20 ft holds '10 of the 48 x 40 size' on the floor; the tool's own planner packs 9, and by hand only 9 fit a 5,898 x 2,352 mm floor (two pallets across means 1016+1016 or 1016+1219 mm; 4 x 1219 + 5 x 1016 along the length).
evidence.fitness: Job walked through: a small exporter with mixed cartons, fragile glassware and floor-only Euro pallets asks how many 40 ft or 40 HC containers to book and whether palletising helps. They get a verified count, a lower bound, a swap table priced at their own quotes, and a printable to-scale plan in seconds; for the README's stated job ('how many containers to book') it is usable. The plan as a stuffing instruction is weaker: the packer has no weight-distribution objective, so 8 x 1,500 kg crates with 40 light ones in a 40 ft land at the back wall (centre of gravity 21% from the back, 96% of the weight in the back half; `node /tmp/claude-0/audit-container/run2.mjs`) and the tool tells the user to 'Move heavy lines toward the middle' with no way to do so on the page; a 235 cm crate is placed in a 20 ft with no note about the door opening.
evidence.domain: Compared with load-planning practice (CTU Code guidance that the cargo's centre of gravity sit near the middle of the length and across the width; door aperture; road weight on chassis; extreme-point heuristics after Crainic, Perboli and Tadei 2008). The packing method, support ratio, load-on-top propagation and payload logic are sound and the counts match standard pallet patterns. Departures: (1) balance is checked after packing, never optimised, and the 10% length / 5% width / 60% height tolerances are uncited planning figures; (2) no door-aperture check (a 2,350 mm crate goes into a 20 ft whose door opening is typically about 2,280 mm high; disclosed in the not-modelled list); (3) 40 ft payload 26,500 kg with no road-weight note, though on a standard US chassis cargo is usually held near 44,000 lb (about 20 t) - disclosed only generically ('any road ... limit'); (4) no floor concentrated-load check; (5) 53 ft preset width is the outside width. Standards cited from own knowledge, not fetched.

defects.what: The FAQ (visible and FAQPage JSON-LD, on the tool page and the guide) says a 20 ft container floor holds about '10 of the 48 x 40 size'; the tool's own planner packs 9 and by hand only 9 fit a 5,898 x 2,352 mm floor (4 x 1,219 + 5 x 1,016 mm columns). A shipper reading the search snippet books for one pallet more than fits.

The packer has no weight-distribution objective: heavy lines are placed first at the back wall (8 x 1,500 kg + 40 x 50 kg in a 40 ft -> COG 21% from the back, 96% of weight in the back half) and the tool then says 'Move heavy lines toward the middle' with no control to do so; the printable plan 'for the warehouse' carries the unbalanced load.

No door-aperture check: a 2,350 mm tall crate is placed in a 20 ft (inside height 2,393 mm, typical door opening about 2,280 mm) with no note. Disclosed in the not-modelled list, but it is the first thing a load planner checks for tall units.

40 ft and 40 HC payload 26,500 kg with no road-weight note; on a standard US chassis cargo is usually held near 44,000 lb (about 20 t), so a 26.4 t plan passes silently. Disclosed only as 'any road ... limit'.
53 ft trailer preset width 2,591 mm (102 in) is the legal outside width; inside is about 99-101 in. The '26 ft box truck' preset is 7,300 mm (about 24 ft) long. Neither cites a source.
Balance tolerances (10% length, 5% width) and the 40 HC height preset are unpinned: doubling either tolerance or cutting the HC height by 100 mm leaves all 77 tests green.
num() strips every comma, so a decimal-comma entry such as '12,5' kg becomes 125 kg silently instead of an error.

The slide step pushes every unit to the left wall (y = 0), so a load narrower than the container is left-justified and the tool flags its own plan as side-heavy (24 x 1,000 kg in a 40 ft: 7% toward the left wall).

verdict: The packing is right: nine recomputed counts (Euro and 48x40 floor patterns in 20 ft, 40 ft, 53 ft and a 26 ft truck, stacked pallets in 40 ft and 40 HC, a payload-bound 600 kg case, and a 255-carton mixed-orientation layer) all match hand geometry, every plan passes the independent verifier, and a hand attempt to beat its 2-trailer answer for the example failed. 77 tests pass and 4 of 7 seeded mutants are caught; balance thresholds and preset sizes are unpinned. It misses the bar on claims: the FAQ on both pages says a 20 ft floor takes about 10 pallets of 48 x 40 in, which the tool itself and hand geometry put at 9. As a stuffing plan a load planner would also stop at weight distribution (heavy units go to the back wall and the tool can only warn), the missing door-aperture check and the silent 26.5 t road weight; all are disclosed as not modelled. For its stated job, how many containers to book, a forwarder could use it.
